title: Prompt engineering
objectives: write an instruction the model can actually follow
show the format instead of describing it
say what to do rather than what to avoid
debug a prompt that stopped working

steps.instruction: Same model, same question. The only difference is the system prompt.
body: No instruction at all. You get a sentence, when you wanted a word.
Nothing is broken. You just did not say what you wanted.
steps.keypoint: With no instruction, you get whatever shape it feels like.

steps.instruction: The system prompt says answer in one word. What comes back?
steps.after: Four words of English. No code changed. That is the whole discipline.
opts: The capital of France is Paris.
steps.why: Four words of English changed the shape of the output. No code changed.

steps.instruction: A prompt that works has three parts. Most broken prompts are missing one.

rules.text: Who it is talking to. A beginner, a teacher, a machine reading JSON.
What to do. One task, said plainly.
rules.example: Explain the error in their code.

rules.text: What shape to answer in. Length, format, what to leave out.

body: The one people skip is the third, and it is the one that makes output unusable.
"Explain this" is a task with no shape, so you get whatever length it fancies.
steps.keypoint: Audience, task, shape. Missing the shape is why output is unusable.

steps.instruction: Audience, task, shape, all three in one prompt.
steps.after: Audience, task, shape. The shape is the part that changed the output.
body: The shape is the part people leave out, and it is the part that makes output usable.

steps.instruction: Now the strongest single trick. Show it, do not describe it.
body: Describing a format: "return the answer as a short lowercase tag".
Showing it: "Example. Input: my chemistry homework. Output: chemistry".
It copies shape far better than it follows description. One example beats a paragraph of rules.
steps.keypoint: One worked example is worth three sentences of instructions.

steps.instruction: Four prompts for the same tagging job. Which returns a consistent format every time?
opts: a, because it is short and leaves room
c, because it shows exactly what the output looks like
d, because it rules out the bad case
steps.why: Concise and not verbose are opinions. An example is a specification: it fixes the length, the case, and the punctuation all at once.
steps.after: The other three all still leave the model guessing what you meant.
steps.keypoint: An example specifies. An adjective only hints.

steps.instruction: Say what to do, not what to avoid.
body: "Do not write a long answer" leaves every length except long.
A ban rules out a corner of the field. An instruction picks the spot.
steps.keypoint: A ban rules out one thing. An instruction picks the one thing.

steps.instruction: Repair this prompt. Swap each ban for an instruction.
steps.after: Both versions mean the same to you. Only one of them is a specification.
steps.keypoint: Positive instructions are testable. Bans are not.
skills: write an instruction the model can follow

steps.instruction: One more, and it is counter-intuitive: give it room to think.
body: On a hard question, demanding the answer alone makes it worse.
"Work through it, then give the answer on the last line" makes it better.
It has no scratchpad. The only place it can work is in the tokens it writes.
steps.keypoint: Its reasoning happens in the output. Leave room for it, then read the last line.

steps.instruction: Which of these gets better when you tell it to work through it first?
opts: Which of these three plans is cheapest, and why
steps.why: Only the plans question has steps in it: compare, weigh, decide. The others are one lookup, and thinking room just costs tokens and time.
steps.after: Room to reason helps multi-step questions. On easy ones it is waste.
steps.keypoint: Give room where there are steps. Not everywhere.

steps.instruction: Deal each line into what it actually does to the output.

items.text: If you are unsure, reply unknown.
This is very important to me.

steps.after: The right column is the encouragement people add when a prompt is not working. It never helps.
steps.keypoint: If a line does not change what a correct answer looks like, delete it.

steps.instruction: Last: your prompt worked for weeks, and today it returns paragraphs.

rules.text: Keep the old prompt. You cannot compare against something you deleted.
Change one thing at a time. Two changes and you learn nothing.
rules.example: add the example OR shorten it

rules.text: Test on the input that broke, not a fresh easy one.
rules.example: the note that produced the paragraph

steps.keypoint: One change, kept versions, tested on the input that actually broke.

steps.after: You did not change a line of code. You changed the English, and the output changed shape.
body: Do not be wordy leaves every length except wordy. Answer in one word leaves one.
Same model, same question. Only the English changed.
